newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BOE's George doubts Germany, France ready for EMU.
newsitem.headline: BOE's George doubts Germany, France ready for EMU.

text.p: Bank of England governor Eddie George doubts Germany and France are ready to join Europe's future economic and monetary union and is arguing for a delay to the 1999 start of EMU, a Belgian newspaper quoted him as saying.

Financial daily De Financieel-Economische Tijd said on Thursday it had been told by George in an interview that chances were that Germany and France would not meet all the convergence criteria in the Maastricht Treaty on EMU unless their economies picked up strongly this year.

Asked whether Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg and Austria could start with EMU in 1999, George said, "I am not certain that the core will be wide as you suggest...the essential question centres on France and Germany."

"From an economic point of view I do not understand why a country which has not yet achieved sustainable convergence already wants to take part in a monetary union and also not why the rest would admit such a country," he said.
"I am afraid that at the moment not enough attention is paid to that sustainability."

A lack of convergence between EMU participants might create large social tensions. "Southern European workers can start asking the same wages as German ones when the currency is identical," the central banker said.
The tensions might trigger plant closures and rising unemployment.
Germany and the Netherlands were "a tandem" which could form a currency union without special risks.
Britain should hold off on joining EMU because of structural differences with the mainland, diverging economic trends and sterling's volatility vis a vis the mark.
George called EMU a divergence when it came to dealing with Europe's main problem: unemployment.

"Fighting unemployment should come from more flexibility in the European economies. In addition almost everybody in Europe agrees that we must keep inflation and government deficits under control. If all European countries base their economic policies firmly on those principles, economically, EMU becomes less important," he said.
